plan.notes: Camera is perfectly front-on (0 azimuth, 0 elevation) to keep the 2D drawing completely flat. authoredPrompt: This figure pairs a flat structural drawing with a three-dimensional model of the same molecule, both cut by a horizontal plane. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" sit one above the other, joined by a vertical bond. The upper carbon bears an "H" above it on a dashed bond, an "HO" group at the left in magenta on a bold wedge, and a "CO2H" group at the right in green. The lower carbon repeats that arrangement flipped vertically: "HO" again at the left and "CO2H" at the right, but its "H" now points downward on a dashed bond. A pale blue parallelogram drawn edge-on slices horizontally between the two carbons, labeled "Symmetry plane". On the right the molecule appears as a ball-and-stick model, two dark gray carbons stacked vertically, each carrying a small blue sphere, a red oxygen with a second red sphere beyond it, and a branching green group, with an identical pale blue plane passing between them. Running the plane through both depictions asks the reader to check one half against the other. Because the halves are reflections, the molecule proves superimposable on its own mirror image despite having two chirality centers, the situation that defines a meso compound.
authoredInteractions:
- Click for selecting an HO, H, or CO2H group on one stereocenter; the reflected counterpart on the other stereocenter highlights across the plane, clarifying why the two halves cancel molecular handedness.
- Toggle between structure-only, model-only, and overlay views of the symmetry plane; the pale plane persists across representations, showing that the same internal reflection explains achirality despite two chirality centers.
authoredContext:
The 2R,3S and 2S,3R structures are identical because the molecule has a plane of symmetry and is therefore achiral. The symmetry plane cuts through the C2–C3 bond, making one half of the molecule a mirror image of the other half (the figure). Because of the plane of symmetry, the molecule is achiral, despite the fact that it has two chirality centers. Such compounds, which are achiral, yet contain chirality centers, are called meso compounds (me-zo). Thus, tartaric acid exists in three stereoisomeric forms: two enantiomers and one meso form.

A symmetry plane through the C2–C3 bond of meso-tartaric acid makes the molecule achiral.

The wedge-dash structure and ball-and-stick model of tartaric acid. C2 and C3 have a horizontal symmetry plane.

Some physical properties of the three stereoisomers are listed in the table. The (+)- and (−)-tartaric acids have identical melting points, solubilities, and densities, but they differ in the sign of their rotation of plane-polarized light. The meso isomer, by contrast, is diastereomeric with the (+) and (−) forms. It has no mirror-image relationship to (+)- and (−)-tartaric acids, is a different compound altogether, and thus has different physical properties.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Coordinates for perfect reflection across y=0 plane: Top Carbon C1 at (0, 1.0, 0). C1-C2 bond goes to C2 at (0, -1.0, 0). Top H at (0, 2.2, -1.0) [up/back]. Top HO at (-1.5, 1.8, 1.0) [up/left/forward]. Top CO2H at (1.5, 1.8, 1.0) [up/right/forward]. Bottom groups mirror exactly: Bottom H at (0, -2.2, -1.0), Bottom HO at (-1.5, -1.8, 1.0), Bottom CO2H at (1.5, -1.8, 1.0). For Side-by-side layout, shift all 2D structure elements to x=-4 and 3D model elements to x=4. Plane is a single y=0 plane spanning x from -7 to 7, z from -3 to 3, pale blue #b3d9ff opacity 0.5. Colors: HO magenta #cc00cc (text) / red #cc0000 (model); CO2H green #008000 (text) / green #33cc33 (model); H teal #008080 (text) / light blue #3399ff (model); C black (text) / dark gray #444444 (model).
interactionPlan.notes: Toggle logic: show/hide the left (Structure) and right (Model) groups based on selection. When toggling to single views, you may smoothly animate their parent groups to x=0 to center them, or just leave them in place. Use THREE.Sprite for text labels in the 2D structure so they always face the camera while orbiting. For the click interaction, pair the meshes (e.g., Top HO and Bottom HO) so clicking either one adds a glowing emissive highlight to both simultaneously.
